#1440. £329m spent and still no goals for sorry Tottenham

Tottenham Hotspur have never before in the club’s history begun a league season without scoring a single goal in the first four games, although having done so after spending £329m on new players really does take some doing.

“Please score a goal!” was the homemade sign from two Spurs fans upon which the television cameras lingered at the end of the game, although the jaunty felt-tip design and glued-on team crest were rather upbeat compared to the gloom of the stadium. Spurs have tried to outrun their past but it just keeps catching up with them.

A team reimagined, a manager freshly launched and yet they are back in the same grip of anxiety that accompanied them on two consecutive 17th-place finishes in the last two seasons. By the end of this they might have been glad to escape with a single point against Everton, the one team in the Premier League who closed the window with a net transfer profit.

For Roberto De Zerbi, there was another passionate defence of his team afterwards. “The people, the fans already understand if I make excuses or not,” he said. “I came last season when the s--- was like this”, he gestured to a level somewhere around the midpoint of his forehead. “I have always been… not positive but realistic. I am sorry for the result that it’s not immediately the improvement. We played as a team. We didn’t score. We didn’t win [but] we played as a team.”

Indeed he co-opted the Italian term “sbloccare” to describe his team’s problem. They simply need to unlock – or unblock – the team and the goals would flow. He joked that in Italy he would be lauded for two consecutive clean sheets in this game and the previous one against Nottingham Forest. “What did you write?” he demanded of one of the Italian newspaper correspondents. “You have the passport.”

Spurs have one last game at home this month, on Saturday against Aston Villa, to end the streak in September. They were into the second half before the first attempt on target that obliged Jordan Pickford to make a save – Mateus Fernandes’s shot slapping limply against the Everton goalkeeper’s gloves to ironic cheers from the home fans.

“There is a term in Italian, ‘sbloccare’ that literally translates as ‘unblock’… I know we can score goals and win games. We have to respect the history of the players – if you forget [Dominic] Solanke and [Omar] Marmoush the others haven’t scored many in their careers. I think we can find the goals with the quality of the players.”

Spurs play Liverpool at Anfield in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday before Villa a week today. The Spurs record at home is dismal. In the last 35 games they have won just five, drawn 10 and lost a remarkable 20. This new stadium has become a problem for the team in it – or maybe it is the other way around.

A good result for Everton, who were under pressure for most of the first half but had much the better of it after the break. David Moyes’s team finished the game with more shots on target than the home team. Moyes managed the game well and trusted his team to withstand the Spurs possession in the first half until they reached a point where Everton could start to push back.

Hard to pick out any major chances – it was that kind of game – but Brennan Johnson should have won it for the away team in the second half. The ball was cut back to him by Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall and the former Spurs man skied his shot.

Some surprised faces then when Moyes said later that he had expected a lot more from his team. He acknowledged the resilience in defence and the importance of the clean sheet. “We played well enough,” he said, “but when we had the ball we turned it over more often than we should have done.”

The game had started with Vitaliy Mykolenko being tortured by the pace of Sávio and ended with the Ukrainian left-back being given the man of the match award. Like many of his team-mates, he had hung in there. There was another fine performance from Jarrad Branthwaite at centre-half and Moyes said that he hoped it might earn him a place in the England squad. “He is still finding his way back from injury,” Moyes said, “it would be great if he could get a call-up.”

In the directors’ box were the usual pained expressions of Vinai Venkatesham, the Spurs chief executive, and chairman Peter Charrington. They sat alongside Vivienne Lewis, daughter of the patriarch Joe. There is a certain fatigue about the home crowd when faced with afternoons like this which suggests they have seen so much that the bar is quite high – or low – to provoke a really splenetic response. Perhaps it is just too early in the season although the final whistle was met with boos.

The first shot on target of the entire game for either side was a free-kick struck by James Garner in added time at the end of the first half. Spurs had started at a ferocious pace although they could not sustain it.

De Zerbi complained about the pre-season injuries on tour in Australia and also the lack of time he had to integrate Sávio and Marmoush. He said that his team were not in the right “physical condition”.

“We played very well in the first 30 minutes and maybe the energy and the fact we didn’t score – we lost confidence.” By the end, he had sent on James Maddison, Tel, Lucas Bergvall and Mohammed Kudus to little avail. Everton looked more likely to win it.

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Everton defender said: “You look at the game from the start, they put us under pressure and we had to dig deep to stay in the game. Then we grew into the game towards the end of the first half and showed that mentality again in the second half.

“We had chances to win the game as well. The backs to the wall mentality will help us go a long way. If we can keep clean sheets, you can go a long way in the league. But it’s not just us the defenders. It’s the whole team working hard. It’s a team effort.”

"I feel like we could've taken three points" James Tarkowski speaks after his sides draw with Spurs 🎙️ pic.twitter.com/Wdj3N5hk8l

"Six hours and we've not scored a goal? It's a DISGRACE" 😬Ashley Young says that the Spurs players will need to have conversations about their lack of threat going forward ❌ pic.twitter.com/0KNomGEavx

"Absolutely diabolical" 😬Jamie Redknapp on Spurs not scoring in their first four Premier League games 😳 pic.twitter.com/48Nbxymlev

Tottenham failed to take the attacking initiative or create any notable chances. De Zerbi used multiple forward players in a host of attacking positions, but no one could find the breakthrough.

Boos ring around the ground as Spurs and Everton both have to settle for a point. Tottenham’s winless start to the season continues, while Everton’s unbeaten run remains intact. Spurs haven’t managed a goal in six hours of Premier League football across the 2026-27 campaign. Tottenham sit 17th with two points. Everton are up to seventh and will certainly take the draw.

FULL-TIME: The points are shared between Spurs and Everton at Tottenham Hotspur stadium 🤝 pic.twitter.com/HwPuKI3Ajh

Dewsbury-Hall’s deflected effort flies out for a corner. Everton can’t make the most of the resulting set piece and Tottenham survive.

There will be three minutes of added time. Are we set for late drama at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium?

Pickford makes an error as his poor clearance is intercepted by Maddison. The ball is eventually worked to Bergvall, whose curling effort is parried away by the Everton goalkeeper.

Jordan Pickford gets down well to deny Lucas Bergvall! 🧤 pic.twitter.com/59uoHTqto6

Tosin comes on for his Spurs debut as he replaces Gray. Can anyone be Tottenham’s hero and find a late winner?

Garner is booked after he clatters into Savio. Everton have produced a tough and disciplined defensive perfomance so far.

Spurs are now enjoying a sustained period of possession. They’re waiting to fashion a big chance and end their wait for a top-flight goal in the 2026-27 season.

De Zerbi makes another change as Maddison enters the action with applause from the Spurs faithful. He replaces Marmoush. It looks like Tel is now operating as a false nine.

Johnson misses a huge chance! Dewsbury-Hall fires a low cross into his path and Johnson takes the chance with a first-time shot, but he slices his effort and it goes over the bar. He’s got to do better from that range inside the penalty area.

That opportunity is Johnson’s last action of the match as he comes off for Hackney. O’Brien is also introduced, replacing Maitland-Niles.

That was the chance. Dewsbury-Hall rolls it into the path of Spurs’ Europa League final winner Brennan Johnson and he skied it. He hasn’t scored since he left Spurs in January for Palace.

"What a chance this was!"Brennan Johnson had the chance to put Everton in front against his former club 😯 pic.twitter.com/fUi7t6hX7t

Everton look like the far likelier side to break the deadlock. De Zerbi’s changes have done little to affect the game. Marmoush is cutting a very frustrated figure up top for Spurs.

Bergvall finds Savio with a whipped cross. The winger tries to help the ball back into the danger zone, but Pickford reacts quickly and collects possession.

Dewsbury-Hall picks up the game’s first yellow card after catching Tonali with a late sliding challenge.

What is Kinsky doing?! The goalkeeper’s dreadful pass which was intended for Tonali is intercepted by Dewsbury-Hall, who tries to slide a low effort through Kinsky’s legs. The Tottenham man redeems himself with a crucial save to keep the scoreline goalless. The hosts are living so dangerously. Kinsky needs to wake up.

Antonín Kinský redeems himself after Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall fails to take advantage! 😮 pic.twitter.com/nuKZju90Wz

Moyes responds with a straight swap on the wing as Grealish comes on for George.

Enter: Grealish. He is on for Tyrique George. Surprised that Brennan Johnson survived that change. He has struggled to make an impression.

Following Spurs’ reshuffle, it looks like Savio will stay out wide on the right, with Tel on the left. Kudus will sit as the central playmaker behind Marmoush, who is now the lone frontman.

De Zerbi orders a much-needed triple change as Kudus, Tel and Bergvall replace Solanke, Fernandes and Bentancur.

Jack Grealish has long since stopped the warm-up on the touchline and is now just staring at the game in expectation of his introduction.

A couple of chances for Everton. Spurs have survived but they look so vulnerable when Everton turn over possession. Crowd could turn soon. Almost reached the hour-mark on matchday 4 and still no Spurs’ Premier League goal.

The start of Spurs’ second-half performance is alarmingly similar to their display against Newcastle two weeks ago. That day, Tottenham allowed Newcastle to seize the initiative and they netted two second-half goals without reply. Everton are gaining confidence as Spurs continue to lack courage or threat. The crowd is getting more and more restless.

Tottenham fail to clear a corner and the ball lands at George’s feet. The Everton winger shoots but his fierce drive is blocked by Bentancur. The whole of Spurs’ bench is warming up. The visitors currently have the momentum and the hosts look nervous.

Everton are looking threatening once again as George attempts to thread a pass through to Johnson on the counter-attack, but Van de Ven is there to clear.

George does brilliantly to escape away from Gray and floats a cross towards the back post. Barry rises highest and his close-range header is blocked by Kinsky. The Tottenham goalkeeper didn’t know much about it, but that’s a massive stop. Undoubtedly the game’s most dangerous moment in front of goal so far.

Spurs’ first shot has arrived! Unfortunately, Fernandes’ tame long-range effort is easily gathered by Pickford. There were some sarcastic cheers from the Tottenham fans as Fernandes took aim. They clearly want more attacking inspiration from their players.

Ironic cheers as Spurs have their first shot on target. It has taken them until the start of the second half and it would be hard to say Fernandes stung the palms of Pickford.

We are back under way for the second half. Everton and Spurs are both unchanged at the break. With the anxiety building in the stadium as the game remains goalless, how long will De Zerbi wait before making a change?

An uneventful first half of football comes to a close. In a game lacking rhythm, creativity and attacking spark, nothing separates Tottenham and Everton at the break. Spurs’ search for a first Premier League goal this season continues.

There will be two added minutes. Everton have a free kick on the edge of Spurs’ penalty area. Garner and Dewsbury-Hall are standing over it. The former Manchester United and Nottingham Forest midfielder takes it and his effort bounces in front of Kinsky, who pushes it out for a corner.

James Garner free-kick pushed away by Kinsky is the game’s first attempt on target.

There has not been a single attempt on target at 40:27 from either team. Spurs have had the best of it but even so. That’s a poor return.

Another attack fizzles out for Spurs. Substitute Jack Grealish engaging in some badinage with home fans as he warms up. He famously agreed a move to Spurs in 2018, called off at the eleventh hour when Aston Villa were sold to the current ownership.

That is so poor from Fernandes. The summer signing’s overhit corner drifts out for a goal kick. Suddenly, Spurs’ attacking play has fallen quite flat.

Pickford does well to intercept Robertson’s inviting low cross. The left back needed Solanke or Marmoush to make a darting near-post run there to give him more options.

Spurs are bossing this game but on the rare occasions Everton escape you do wonder if they might score.

Tottenham are roared on by the home support to move the ball a bit quicker going forward. Out of possession, Everton almost revert to a back five, with Garner dropping very deep near to Tarkowski and Branthwaite.

Tonali picks out Gray with a pinpoint pass. Garner is alert to the danger and tracks back to clear, stopping Gray from getting a one-on-one opportunity.

Maitland-Niles does very well to dispossess Tonali in a dangerous area, allowing Barry to tee up Dewsbury-Hall, but his shot is smothered by the Spurs defence. Mykolenko then chips a cross into a box, but it’s tapped behind for a corner by Robertson. Moyes will certainly be encouraged by this side’s resurgence over the last 10 minutes.

There is a break in play here with Gray down and receiving treatment after a collision. He appears to be holding his lower back. The Tottenham man gingerly gets back to his feet and trudges off the pitch.

Gray down for some extended treatment. Richarlison in the stands. Spurs in danger of losing early momentum.

After Spurs’ fast start, Everton have grown into the contest over the last five minutes and are getting on the ball far higher up the pitch.

Garner’s corner is cleared by Spurs, but only as far as Maitland-Niles. In similar range to where he scored that stunning equaliser against Manchester United, the former Arsenal man shoots, but his attempt fizzes well wide.

Spurs are really flowing here. Finding the balls through the lines and real speed when they attack Everton. Big question is whether they can convert that into goals. Van Hecke and Fernandes both had chances.

Sávio has had a fine start to the game. Mykolenko in for a long afternoon. Spurs have looked dangerous and should be 1-0 up.

Tonali finds Savio with a deep cross, leaving Pickford in no-man’s land. The Brazilian keeps the ball in play and it loops up, just out of Marmoush’s reach.

Robertson floats a teasing delivery into Van Hecke at the back post, but the centre-back directs his half-volley over the bar from close range.

Spurs then burst forward again through Savio, who feeds Fernandes. The playmaker’s low drive is heroically blocked by Tarkowski as Everton continue to hold on (just about).

As expected, it’s Tottenham with all the early possession, with Everton sitting very deep and soaking up the early pressure. Marmoush turns Armstrong and wins a free-kick in a dangerous area.

They’re under way in north London, the hosts are in their lily-white and navy kit, with Everton in their grey/dirty green (is that a colour?!) away number.

Greetings from N17. It’s a wonderful, warm late summer evening. As expected there is the usual foreboding from the home fans. Two defeats and one draw. The mood will sour further if Spurs do not win today. No Porro or Udogie so Archie Gray, ever adaptable, starts at right-back again.

Everton are undefeated with five points from three games. They have a decent 16/17 players but it is the reserves beyond that which everyone is concerned about. Grealish and Dibling on the bench give them two potential game-changers. Spurs’ squad looks very strong on the team-sheet. A full bench of experienced pros and no fillers. On the pitch it has been less convincing.

"Solanke is a crucial player"Roberto De Zerbi on the importance of Dominic Solanke being fit for Spurs 💪 pic.twitter.com/FNWNsTWdt8

Coventry City vs Brighton & Hove Albion (14:00)

Manchester United vs Manchester City (16:30)

Brennan Johnson spent two years at Tottenham and scored the winning goal in the 1-0 Europa League final victory over Manchester United in May 2025, ending the club’s 17-year trophy drought.

After a short, disappointing spell at Crystal Palace, Johnson joined Everton last month, with Dwight McNeil moving in the opposite direction.

The Welsh winger starts for Everton today. Could he hurt his previous employers on a day where they desperately need a win?

Brennan in the building. 💙 pic.twitter.com/94GgAY8c56

Midfielder took exception to negativity surrounding club after moves for players on deadline day failed to materialise.

“We signed Jack [Grealish], which was nice, and I’d been speaking to him,” says Dewsbury-Hall, sitting in a café at the club’s Finch Farm training base. “But I had seen all the stuff [online], all the meltdowns about this and that and, in all honestly, it annoyed me a bit.

“I get where people are coming from. Everyone wants to sign everyone and have the perfect squad, but there are still 19 lads in this building who are going to hopefully take this club to good things this year. That was getting disregarded. I was seeing people saying: ‘We’ll be lucky to stay up this year.’

“What message is that sending to the lads who are already here? I’m not blaming anyone. We get it. It didn’t work. But let’s all be positive – right, it’s done, bang, let’s go. That’s what we’ve been trying to say in the dressing room.”

Earlier this week, Mykhailo Mudryk picked up an ankle injury in training which has ruled the Chelsea loanee out of action for as long as two months.

The winger only made his debut for Tottenham as a late substitute against Nottingham Forest last week, but his attempt to rebuild his career following his anti-doping ban has been dealt a major blow.

Folarin Balogun’s proposed £39m move from Monaco collapsed on transfer deadline day, Richarlison’s return to the club didn’t materialise and Beto was sold to Fiorentina, leaving Thierno Barry as Everton’s only recognised striker.

Nottingham Forest’s pursuit of academy product Harrison Armstrong ruffled the fans’ feathers, while Iliman Ndiaye was sold to Manchester City for £60m.

Dwight McNeil, Tim Iroegbunam, Nathan Patterson, Adam Aznou and Idrissa Gueye were also allowed to leave.

Merlin Rohl and Tyrique George made their loans permanent, while Brennan Johnson, Hayden Hackney and Christian Norgaard were also added to the squad.

Summer signing Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Vitaliy Mykolenko are David Moyes’ only options at full-back.

Overall, there were a number of solid additions, just not enough of them to cover all the departures.

🎧🫡 Thierno Barry ahead of today's clash in North London. pic.twitter.com/mwlsKH8Pid

Tottenham: Kinsky; Gray, Van de Ven, Van Hecke, Robertson; Tonali, Bentancur, Fernandes; Savio, Solankem, Marmoush.

Subs: Dubravka, Tosin, Senesi, Gallagher, Maddison, Tel, Bergvall, Kudus, Davies.

Everton: Pickford; Maitland-Niles, Tarkowski, Brathwaite, Mykolenko; Armstrong, Garner; Johnson, Dewsbury-Hall, George; Barry.

Subs: Travers, O’Brien, Keane, King, Alcaraz, Graham, Hackney, Dibling, Grealish.

After scoring that last-minute leveller against Manchester United last time out, Ainsley Maitland-Niles is promoted to the starting 11 and replaces Merlin Rohl. Brennan Johnson returns to his former club and starts, while Jack Grealish is on the bench.

Today's Toffees to face @SpursOfficial. COYB! ✊#TOTEVE pic.twitter.com/mOcCayRUfm

Roberto De Zerbi has made four alterations from last weekend’s stalemate with Nottingham Forest. Dominic Solanke, Mateus Fernandes, Archie Gray and Andy Robertson all come into the line-up. Pedro Porro and Destiny Udogie are out injured, while Conor Gallagher and Mathys Tel are relegated to the bench. Tosin Adarabioyo and James Maddison are also among the substitutes.

Our Spurs side to take on Everton 👊🔢 @krakenfx pic.twitter.com/n637s7swiD

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League meeting between Tottenham and Everton in the capital.

Are Tottenham in must-win territory already? It may seem reactionary and premature, but after spending £380m in the summer to revamp an underperforming squad, Tottenham sit inside the relegation zone, with just one point and zero goals scored in three games.

Roberto De Zerbi’s men opened the 2026-27 top-flight season with worrying back-to-back defeats to Brentford and Newcastle United, before ending their losing streak last weekend thanks to a goalless draw against Nottingham Forest.

This game gives Tottenham another opportunity to reverse their dreadful home form. Last season, Spurs managed just three league wins at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium and lost 10. The recent 2-0 loss against Newcastle was a painful reminder of Spurs’ shortcomings at home, but they’ll be expected to be authoritative and seize the initiative here today. A much-needed three points would be the perfect remedy to ease the pressure and unwanted attention on De Zerbi and his squad.

Meanwhile, Everton have made an unbeaten start to the season, accumulating five points from their first three league matches. David Moyes’ side looked set for defeat last time out, when they were trailing Manchester United 2-1 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium heading into stoppage time, until Ainsley Maitland-Niles’ stunning 96th-minute equaliser salvaged a draw.

Alongside drama on the pitch, there has also been noise off it. A bizarre transfer window has left Everton with a serious lack of depth up top and in both full-back positions. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall responded to the fans’ negativity over this situation, saying their meltdowns “annoyed” him.

Nevertheless, they arrive in North London with all eyes on Tottenham and if the hosts can find a first league victory this season.

Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1439. Matchday Guide: Everton v Coventry

Fans are strongly advised to arrive early as Everton host Coventry City in the Premier League at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Friday 6 November (8pm kick-off).

This game marks Everton’s annual Remembrance fixture, which will see a tribute take place ahead of kick-off involving representatives from the Armed Forces, the laying of commemorative poppy wreaths in memory of the fallen and a rendition of The Last Post. More details on the Remembrance ceremony can be found HERE.

Supporters are advised to plan their journey in advance due to ongoing engineering works taking place on the Merseyrail network, which will entail replacement bus services operating between Hunts Cross and Moorfields (NB: there is no rail replacement bus stop by Liverpool Central).

Train services will be running as usual between Southport, Ormskirk and Headbolt Lane & Liverpool Central, and return journeys. For the latest updates Merseyrail, click HERE

On the approach to the stadium, Boundary Street is currently down to one lane due to emergency gas works.  Boundary Street will continue to operate as a one-way street in the direction of Hill Dickinson Stadium in the three hours prior to kick-off, minimising disruption for matchday traffic and bus services. However, supporters are advised to leave more time for their journey in case of delays in and around this route.

Some key information follows, and for everything else you need ahead of your visit - including general travel information, food and drink options, digital ticketing support, accessibility guidance and more on what’s happening around the stadium - visit evertonfc.com/matchday.

9am - The Ticket Office opens until half-time. The away ticket office, located outside the North Stand, will open at 5pm.

5pm - Access to the stadium site opens via the Regent Road wall, with food and drink outlets on the Budweiser Plaza. All available gates (A–E) in the Regent Road wall will be open and supporters are encouraged to use the full range of entrances to help avoid unnecessary congestion.

6pm - Stadium turnstiles open, with food and drink available across all concourses, including Early Bird offers until 6pm. Please ensure your digital match ticket has been downloaded to your mobile device before arriving at the stadium. A step-by-step digital ticketing guide and stadium map can be found HERE.

7.50pm – Remembrance service sees service armed forces personnel, standard bearers and veterans escorted pitchside ready for commencement, upon team walk-outs.

9.50pm - Following the end of the game, the South Stand Bar will remain open for one hour for supporters, with Level 0 open for 30 minutes (see below for more).

NB: Following the game, supporters should leave Hill Dickinson Stadium using the designated exit gates (A–E) on the Regent Road wall. The Nelson Dock exit, accessed from the Budweiser Plaza, is reserved exclusively for supporters with allocated parking in this area, including supporters using accessible parking. Please note, there will be no pedestrian access from Nelson Dock onto Regent Road after the game.

Please be advised that a short period of flashing lights will take place ahead of the teams taking to the pitch. Fans with photosensitive disorders, sensitivity to strobing lights, or who may react to flashing lights, may wish to remain in the concourse until this activation has concluded. Lighting will return to normal as the players emerge on the pitch.

Early bird deals, available inside the stadium for the first 60 minutes following turnstiles opening, are as follows:

Salt and Pepper Chicken Sharebox & 2 pints of & San Miguel for £30 (Flight Birds)

Salt and Pepper Chicken Sharebox & 2 pints of Budweiser - £28 (Flight Birds).

The Upper South Stand bar will remain open for one hour after the final whistle.

All supporters on Level 2 can access this bar after the game and, subject to capacity and operational requirements, home supporters from lower areas will also be able to access the bar post-match. This will be via the Lower South escalators for fans on Level 0, or via pass gates at Entrance 7a if coming from other areas of the stadium.

Please note, supporters on Level 0 will not be allowed to access Level 2 until it is safe to do so. A bar on Level 0 will be open for supporters for 30 minutes while they wait for the Upper Tier crowd to disperse and for access to be granted.

Everton has introduced a new digital service that will allow supporters to access Audio Description Commentary through their own mobile devices when attending matches at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

The technology – accessed via a web link - enables blind and partially-sighted supporters to listen to live Audio Description Commentary (ADC) through the flexibility of their own smartphone and headphones, removing the need to collect and return a separate receiver and offering a more seamless and independent matchday experience.

Fans wishing to access the new service should visit the Accessibility Ticket Office on matchday, where members of the Club's accessibility team will help them download the app and get connected.

NB: Supporters will need to bring their own headphones compatible with their mobile device to use the service.

For further information on Hill Dickinson Stadium’s accessible provision, click here or contact accessibility@evertonfc.com

We hope you enjoy your visit to Hill Dickinson Stadium.

If you see or hear anything that does not feel right, please report it to a steward or police officer. In an emergency, call 999.

#1438. Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Algal bloom demise, often caused by viruses, is a major driver of carbon cycling in the surface ocean1,2. However, although blooms collapse synchronously, fewer than 30% of algal cells are actively infected by viruses3, indicating the involvement of additional mortality agents. Here we quantified tripartite interactions within a synthetic community composed of the abundant coccolithophore Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, bacteria and viruses isolated during a bloom. We found that bacteria significantly enhanced virus-induced algal mortality in G. huxleyi as well as in three other globally widespread microalgae. We quantified this interaction using two new metrics: the synergy index, which measures viral–bacterial interaction strength, and the benefit index, which assesses changes in bacterial fitness. We identified Alteromonas bacteria as drivers of viral–bacterial co-infection, with consistently high synergy index and benefit index. We found that during algal blooms, Alteromonas displayed high chemoattraction towards infected cell extracts, accumulated in aggregates derived from bloom demise, and increased in abundance during oceanic bloom collapse. Viral–bacterial synergy represents a previously unrecognized mortality agent that controls bloom termination, modulating the balance between the carbon-recycling viral shunt and the carbon-exporting viral shuttle pathways, which influence global carbon cycling4,5,6.

About 50 gigatons of carbon are fixed annually by marine phototrophs, feeding the entire microbial food web7,8,9. A substantial portion of this carbon fixation occurs during large-scale algal blooms1,10. Therefore, microbial processes that control cell fate in these blooms can have profound effects on marine carbon cycling11. Algal blooms are hotspots for diverse interactions and metabolic exchange with grazers, bacteria, fungi and viruses12,13. Marine viruses, the most abundant biological entities in the ocean, are major mortality agents, driving nutrient cycling globally and significantly impacting algal bloom demise2,14,15.

Viruses regulate the fate of carbon and other nutrients16 through two distinct ecosystem processes: the viral shunt4,5, which fuels the microbial food web by catalysing nutrient recycling in the surface ocean; and the viral shuttle5,6, which facilitates carbon export through enhanced aggregation of lysed cells and sinking of particulate organic matter in the oligotrophic ocean17 and during algal blooms18. Viral lysis of algal populations creates a distinct metabolic footprint19,20,21, which can promote the growth of adapted heterotrophs22, thereby altering microbial biodiversity23,24. Yet, how virus-induced shifts in microbial community composition influence algal cell fate—and thus global carbon cycling—remains poorly understood.

We selected G. huxleyi (previously known as Emiliania huxleyi) to study algae–virus–bacteria interactions owing to its ecological significance in marine ecosystems. This cosmopolitan unicellular eukaryotic alga forms extensive blooms, covering thousands of square kilometers25. It has a crucial role in global carbon and sulfur biogeochemical cycles due to its carbon fixation, its calcite exoskeleton production, and the release of sulfur volatiles such as dimethyl sulfide25,26,27. These blooms are often terminated following infection by a giant double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) virus, the Emiliania huxleyi virus (EhV)28. Despite the observed synchronized collapse of entire blooms29, quantification of active viral infection using single-cell approaches revealed a discrepancy: fewer than 30% of algal cells were infected by the virus during the bloom’s demise3,30. This suggests that additional mortality agents may act together with viral infection. Inspired by findings from the biomedical field demonstrating that viral–bacterial co-infections synergistically increase mortality31,32, we investigated the interplay between bacteria and viruses during algal bloom demise. Using a bacterial consortium isolated from natural algal blooms (Extended Data Fig. 1), we showed that bacteria can exacerbate virus-induced algal mortality, revealing a previously unrecognized tripartite interaction with potentially important implications for global biogeochemical cycles.

We sought to determine the role of bacteria as additional mortality agents during virus-induced algal bloom demise. We hypothesized that if bacteria that are naturally associated with an alga contribute to its mortality, then an antibiotic treatment would reduce the overall death rate during viral infection. To test this idea, we cultured a xenic strain of G. huxleyi isolated from a bloom induced during a mesocosm experiment near Bergen, Norway24. In the absence of viral infection, the xenic cultures subjected to the antibiotic treatment showed up to 1.2-fold higher algal growth (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 2a), indicating that under normal growth conditions, bacteria naturally associated with G. huxleyi maintain a competitive relationship. Infection with EhV induced algal population decline from day 1 (Fig. 1a). However, when antibiotics were administered to reduce the abundance of the algal microbiome (Extended Data Fig. 2a), we observed reduced algal mortality, up to 19-fold, compared with cultures that were not treated with antibiotics (linear mixed-effects model, P < 0.05 from day 2; Fig. 1a). This difference suggests that the bacterial community may contribute significantly to algal mortality during viral infection, indicating a potential synergistic pathogenic interaction between viruses and bacteria. Analysis of bacterial abundance revealed that bacteria grew to 1.5-fold higher abundance in the virus-infected cultures compared with the uninfected condition (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4 from day 4; Fig. 1b). The differences in viral production between antibiotic-treated and untreated algal cultures were significant during the days of viral release, but the abundances leveled off resulting in similar total abundances (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05 on day 4 and day 6; Fig. 1c).

Dynamics of xenic alga–virus interactions for G. huxleyi (Gh) (a–c), P. globosa (Pg) (d), M. commoda (Mc) (e) and O. tauri (Ot) (f). a,d–f, Growth curves of uninfected and virus-infected xenic algal cultures with or without antibiotic (Ab) treatment. b, Bacterial abundances in uninfected and virus-infected G. huxleyi cultures. c, Viral abundances in antibiotics-treated and untreated G. huxleyi cultures. Statistical significance determined by a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per time point. Data are mean ± s.d. (n = 4 independent cultures for G. huxleyi and n = 3 for all other species). *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001; NS, not significant (P ≥ 0.05). Exact P values are provided in the Source data.

To determine the generality of our findings, we assessed whether such synergistic pathogenic interactions occur for other marine microalgae whose bloom demise is controlled by viral infections, namely Phaeocystis globosa, Micromonas commoda and Ostreococcus tauri33,34,35. The mortality of all three algae was significantly attenuated when treating virus-infected, xenic algal cultures with antibiotics (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 1d–f). These results demonstrate that viral–bacterial synergy leading to algal mortality is a widespread phenomenon among key marine algal species. Notably, antibiotic treatment did not reduce the mortality of O. tauri upon infection with a specialist virus (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 2e), possibly owing to the rapid recovery of a resistant population. This exemplifies that the extent of viral–bacterial synergy may depend on various factors such as host susceptibility, viral infectivity and microbiome composition. We propose that bacteria and viruses kill synergistically, whereby viral infection creates favourable conditions for bacterial pathogenicity, accelerating algal mortality and fuelling bacterial growth. Thus, bacteria naturally associated with G. huxleyi and other cosmopolitan microalgae can expedite their bloom demise during viral infection.

We sought to disentangle the interactions between algae, viruses and bacteria during algal bloom demise. To this end, we developed a tripartite laboratory model system using algal, viral and bacterial strains that were isolated from an algal bloom (Extended Data Fig. 1). We isolated the bloom-associated microbiome (BAM) from the demise phase and determined its effect on G. huxleyi during viral infection.

We next reconstituted the tripartite system by exposing axenic G. huxleyi cultures to EhV with and without the BAM community, and observed an enhancement of algal mortality in the presence of bacteria (Fig. 2a). Although viral infection alone significantly reduced algal abundance compared with uninfected cultures, the addition of the BAM accelerated this decline, resulting in approximately fourfold lower algal cell densities after 7 days (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 2a). This recapitulated our observations in xenic G. huxleyi cultures (Fig. 1a), confirming that bacterial presence synergistically enhances virus-induced algal mortality.

a, Growth curves of axenic G. huxleyi under four conditions: uninfected, with BAM only, with EhV only and with both BAM and EhV. b, Bacterial abundances in cultures with and without viral infection. c, Viral production in axenic and BAM-inoculated cultures. d, Bacterial community composition of the inoculum (In.) and over time in uninfected (bottom blue line) and EhV-infected (bottom yellow line) cultures. Data are mean ± s.d. (n = 5 independent cultures). Exact P values are provided in the Source data. Statistical significance determined by a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per day.

Bacterial population dynamics revealed significant proliferation in the tripartite system compared with the bacteria-only treatment (Fig. 2b). Similar to xenic G. huxleyi cultures (Fig. 1b), bacterial abundances in the virus-infected cultures were more than threefold higher than in the uninfected cultures 7 days post-infection (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4 from day 2), suggesting that bacterial communities exploit metabolites that are released during viral infection.

By contrast, viral production remained similar between axenic and BAM-supplemented cultures (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Fig. 2c). Additionally, we quantified the effect of BAM supplementation on the fraction of virus-infected algal cells (Extended Data Fig. 3), enumerated at the single-cell level using single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH)3, based on the expression of the viral major capsid protein (mcp) gene. During the lytic phase, up to 70% of algal cells were virus-infected independent of the presence or absence of BAM (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 3d), proportions consistent with previous work with infected G. huxleyi cultures3. These findings suggest that the bacterial consortium augments algal death without affecting viral infection.

To identify whether specific bacteria are driving the synergy of this tripartite interaction, we characterized changes in microbial community composition during viral infection using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (Fig. 2d). The bacterial community changed reproducibly in all replicates during viral infection. Whereas the uninfected cultures maintained a stable community dominated by Marinomonas, a pronounced shift occurred in the virus-infected cultures by day 4, coinciding with algal decline. Notably, the relative abundances of Alteromonas and Olleya increased in the infected cultures, from approximately 2.1 ± 0.3% and 0.01 ± 0.01%, respectively, at the beginning of the experiment (day 1), to 20.2 ± 2.7% and 32.9 ± 4.4% by day 7, thereby dominating the bacterial community (Fig. 2d). Concurrently, Pseudoalteromonas and Yoonia-Loktanella increased in their relative abundances, whereas Marinomonas declined. These findings suggest that viral infection creates a distinct metabolic niche that selectively promotes specific bacterial taxa that are capable of exploiting virus-induced changes in algal metabolism or cell lysis products, as previously shown24,36.

To disentangle the microbial dynamics governing algal bloom demise, we developed two quantitative metrics that assess the contribution of individual bacterial taxa to virus-induced algal mortality, and the effect of viral infection of algal cells on bacterial fitness. The synergy index (SI) quantifies the decrease in the algal population during viral infection in the presence of bacteria compared to viral infection alone. The benefit index (BI) measures the growth advantage that bacteria gain during viral infection compared to their growth with uninfected algae.

To calculate the SI, we use the area under the algal growth curve during viral infection alone (AUCvirus) and during viral–bacterial co-infection (AUCtripartite). We selected area under the curve (AUC) as our metric because it provides a biologically meaningful measure of cumulative biomass change that captures complete temporal dynamics rather than single time points and offers robustness through multiple daily measurements. We calculated the difference between AUCvirus and AUCtripartite and normalized this value using AUCvirus, which is represented mathematically as SI (%) = (AUCvirus − AUCtripartite)/AUCvirus × 100% (Fig. 3a and Methods). Normalizing the differences in the AUC creates a dimensionless metric, enabling direct comparison across bacterial strains and experimental conditions regardless of baseline differences. A positive SI indicates that the bacterial presence reduces algal populations beyond the reduction caused by viruses alone, with higher values reflecting stronger effects (for example, SI = 10.0% means a 10% increase in tripartite-induced algal decline compared to mortality induced by viruses alone). The BAM had an SI of 22.2 ± 2.3%, which confirms the substantial effect of this bacterial community on the virus-induced demise of G. huxleyi (Fig. 3b).

a, Illustration of the SI calculation method, comparing growth curves of virus-infected alga with or without bacteria. b, Application of SI to assess the effect of the entire BAM community, showing significant enhancement of virus-induced mortality of G. huxleyi (SI = 22.2 ± 2.3%). c,d, Representative bacterial isolates from the BAM with contrasting SI values. A. stellipolaris (Ast) MB63 exhibits high (SI = 20.2 ± 2.7%) (c) whereas S. pontiacus (Sp) MB3 exhibits low (SI = 7.8 ± 2.7%) (d) synergistic killing. e, Illustration of the BI calculation, comparing bacterial growth curves in the presence of virus-infected or uninfected alga. f, Application of BI to the entire BAM community (BI = 259.8 ± 17.0%), indicating a substantial growth advantage during viral infection of G. huxleyi. g,h, Bacterial growth curves showing contrasting BI values. A. stellipolaris MB63 derives large benefit (BI = 112.4 ± 1.0%) from co-infection (g), whereas S. pontiacus MB3 shows no advantage (BI = −17.2 ± 3.0%) (h). Dashed lines mark limits for the area integration, excluding the first day which is below detection levels. i, SI and BI values for bacteria isolated directly from the BAM community (black outline) or a G. huxleyi bloom (no outline), revealing diverse ecological strategies. Asp, Alteromonas sp.; Hs, Hyphomonas sp.; Ms, Marinomonas sp.; Os, Olleya sp.; Rm, Roseovarius mucosus; Ss, Sulfitobacter sp. j, Classification of bacterial ecological strategies based on SI and BI values, identifying opportunistic pathogens, killers, consumers and agnostic bacteria (log10(BI) > 0). Data are mean ± s.e.m. (n = 3 independent cultures). Asterisks indicate P values for differences in the growth dynamics as obtained by repeated-measures two-way ANOVA (b–d,f–h); exact P values are provided in the Source data.

The BI quantifies the growth advantage bacteria derive from viral infection, calculated as BI (%) = (AUCtripartite − AUCbacteria)/AUCbacteria × 100%, where AUCbacteria represents the area under the bacterial growth curve with uninfected algae (Fig. 3e). The BAM community exhibited a high BI (259.8 ± 17.0%), indicating that viral infection of G. huxleyi creates a metabolically accessible niche that enhances bacterial proliferation almost fourfold (Fig. 3f).

To identify key contributors to this synergistic interaction, we examined the SI and BI for individual bacteria isolated from the BAM (Supplementary Data 1). Alteromonas stellipolaris MB63 exhibited a high SI (20.2 ± 2.7%), indicating that this species enhanced virus-induced algal population decline by about 20% (Fig. 3c). By contrast, Sulfitobacter pontiacus MB3 had a low, non-significant SI (7.8 ± 2.7%), suggesting that this species is not affecting algal death during viral infection (Fig. 3d). Correspondingly, A. stellipolaris MB63 exhibited a high BI (112.4 ± 1.0%), reflecting more than twofold growth enhancement during viral infection (Fig. 3g), whereas S. pontiacus MB3 showed a slight growth deficit during virus infection (BI = −17.2 ± 3.0%; Fig. 3h).

To expand the taxonomic range of our analysis, we tested a total of 12 bacteria isolated either directly from the BAM community or from the G. huxleyi bloom (Supplementary Data 1), and observed high variability in both metrics (SI range from 5.4% to 23.2% and BI range from −17.2% to 451.0%; Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). The three Alteromonas strains tested (MB63, MB67 and MB68) consistently exhibited a large effect on algal population decline (SI range from 18.6% to 21.7%; Fig. 3i), while simultaneously deriving growth benefits from viral infection (BI range from 18.5% to 112.4%; Fig. 3i).

By mapping all bacterial isolates onto a coordinate system defined by their SI and BI values (the SI–BI phase space), we observed distinct phenotypes (Fig. 3j) and propose a framework comprising four ecological strategies: ‘opportunistic pathogens’ (high SI, high BI), exemplified by Alteromonas species, which both accelerate algal mortality and efficiently exploit the resulting metabolic niche; ‘consumers’ (low SI, high BI), such as Olleya sp. MB6, which derive substantial growth benefits from viral infection without contributing significantly to algal mortality; ‘killers’ (high SI, low BI), including Sulfitobacter sp. MB51, which enhance algal mortality but gain no growth advantage; and ‘agnostics’ (low SI, low BI), such as S. pontiacus MB3, which neither increase algal mortality nor derive substantial growth benefits from viral infection.

To determine whether synergistic bacteria directly affect the mortality of algal cells, we quantified the fraction of dying algal cells during tripartite interaction (Fig. 4a,b and Extended Data Fig. 3). Dying algal cells were identified as cells with compromised membranes using the DNA stain SYTOX Green (Fig. 4a), and were further differentiated by their chlorophyll autofluorescence as metabolically active (high chlorophyll autofluorescence) or metabolically impaired (low chlorophyll autofluorescence) cells (Fig. 4b). During viral infection, there was an accumulation of dying (SYTOX+) cells reaching up to 76.9 ± 2.4% of the algal population (on day 4; Fig. 4a). The addition of bacteria significantly reduced the percentage of dying algal cells (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4) reaching 21.0 ± 1.5% (on day 3; Fig. 4a), suggesting that bacteria selectively remove dying algae during viral infection. Bacteria selectively cleared low-chlorophyll cells versus high-chlorophyll cells. In the presence of bacteria, the percentage of SYTOX+ cells among all low-chlorophyll cells decreased from 54.0 ± 4.1% to 30.3 ± 3.0% on day 2 (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 4b), whereas the percentage of SYTOX+ cells among high-chlorophyll cells remained similar (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Fig. 4b). These findings show that bacteria preferentially remove metabolically impaired dying cells during virus-induced algal demise.

a, Total abundance (grey) and fraction (yellow or red) of membrane-compromised (SYTOX+) algal cells in axenic G. huxleyi cultures inoculated with EhV only (light grey, red) and with both EhV and the BAM community (dark grey, yellow). b, Fraction of SYTOX+ cells that are still metabolically active (high chlorophyll autofluorescence) or dead (low chlorophyll autofluorescence). Statistical significance determined by a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per time point. Exact P values are provided in the Source data. Data are mean ± s.d. (n = 4 independent cultures).

We sought to determine the metabolic basis for viral–bacterial synergy in algal killing. We focused on lipid metabolism since EhV infection profoundly remodels the lipidome of G. huxleyi, inducing triacylglycerol (TAG) production and accumulation of intracellular lipid bodies37. We thus sequenced and annotated the genomes of all bacterial isolates and correlated the SI of each one with the completeness (per cent of genes encoded in the KEGG pathway) of its fatty acid degradation (FAD) pathway. We found a significant positive correlation between SI and the FAD pathway completeness (Spearman’s ρ = 0.669, P = 0.017; Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Data 2). Detailed examination revealed that within the BAM consortium, the species with the highest SI values, all belonging to the genus Alteromonas, also encode the complete enzymatic machinery for TAG hydrolysis and subsequent fatty acid transmembranal transport and β-oxidation, including TAG lipase, fadL, fadD, fadE, fadB and fadA and their homologues (Extended Data Fig. 6b). By contrast, species with low SI values (for example, S. pontiacus MB3) showed several missing enzymes in the FAD pathway. Among bloom-associated bacterial isolates, only Alteromonas and Marinobacter strains encode these metabolic genes (Supplementary Data 2). Although this may be a phylogenetic trait that is not causally related to SI or BI, these genera were recently shown to selectively degrade algal lipids38. Most importantly, Alteromonas encodes a TAG lipase, an enzyme that releases free fatty acids from TAGs for cellular metabolism. This feature may be particularly advantageous during viral infection of G. huxleyi as EhV infection induces the release of extracellular vesicles that are enriched in TAGs39.

Having identified Alteromonas as having key roles in the viral–bacterial synergy during algal demise, we investigated the ecological importance of this genus during natural bloom succession. To this end, we tracked algal, viral and bacterial dynamics in a natural environment, measured daily during G. huxleyi bloom succession in a mesocosm experiment24. Following six days at low abundance (less than 5 × 105 cells per ml; pre-bloom phase), G. huxleyi showed a steady increase in cell numbers (days 7–14; bloom phase) and, upon viral infection (days 15–23; infection phase), its population collapsed (Fig. 5a).

SS, side scatter. b, Relative abundance of indicated bacterial families in planktonic (<2 μm) and particle-attached (>20 μm) fractions. c, Scheme suggesting that bacterial enrichment on particles during the infection phase may be facilitated through chemoattraction towards virus-infected cells. Virus-infected (yellow) and uninfected (green) G. huxleyi cell extracts were used as chemoattractants. Filtered mesocosm water (pink) served as reference.
