The motion of tectonic plates and subduction zones affected mantle convection and dynamic topography12,29,32,33,37,38 (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). At 640 Ma, dynamic topography exhibited a north–south hemispheric planform with positive dynamic topography beneath Laurentia, Baltica, North China, Amazonia, Australia, the Kalahari Craton and Antarctica (Fig. 2a), which were above a BLOBS in the absence of subduction south of 50° S (Fig. 2c). Laurentia was tilted down to the southwest, positioned above whole-mantle upwelling (Fig. 2e). The fast motion of continental blocks and of subduction zones between 600 Ma and 320 Ma (ref. 39) reorganized mantle convection (Supplementary Videos 1 and 2) so that by 440 Ma, the hemispheric planform of dynamic topography was oriented east–west, with negative dynamic topography beneath most continental blocks, including at high latitude in both hemispheres (Fig. 2b). Laurentia was tilted down to the southeast, because of subduction-driven downwelling along its eastern margin and whole-mantle upwelling above a BLOBS in the west (Fig. 2f).

We used k-means cluster analysis to quantify the spatial and temporal evolution of continental dynamic topography during the formation (920–420 Ma) and preservation (420–0 Ma) of the Great Unconformity (Fig. 3 and Methods). We established that considering two clusters for each period was prototypical for most considered model cases except M3 and M5, for which three clusters were appropriate (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 1). These clusters, which we represented in the present-day continental configuration, captured regions in which dynamic topography evolved similarly over time (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 2).

a–c, Spatial distribution of two clusters across continental blocks that existed from 920 Ma: GU-F (Great Unconformity—formation) and GU-NF (Great Unconformity—no formation) between 920 Ma and 420 Ma (a); GU-HPP (Great Unconformity—high preservation potential) and GU-LPP (Great Unconformity—low preservation potential) from 420 Ma (b); regions in which the Great Unconformity was formed and preserved (GU-F/P), as opposed to regions with low formation and preservation potential (GU-NF/LPP) (c). Robinson projection at the surface of Earth. d,e, Temporal evolution of averaged continental dynamic topography for each cluster in a and b, respectively. The black and brown dashed lines represent the average dynamic topography for Laurentia and Baltica, respectively. The vertical dashed line represents the start of Cambrian times, and the horizontal dashed line represents the datum for dynamic topography. d, Averaged continental dynamic topography for clusters GU-F (orange) and GU-NF (grey) between 920 Ma and 420 Ma. The light-blue-shaded regions represent the duration of the two main glaciations during Cryogenian times. e, Averaged continental dynamic topography for clusters GU-HPP (orange) and GU-LPP (grey) from 420 Ma. f, Locations of orogens56 from 900 Ma (coloured by age in 100 Ma intervals). Robinson projection at the surface of Earth.

For the period 920–420 Ma, the main continental blocks in cluster GU-F (Great Unconformity—formation) were Laurentia, Baltica, northeastern North China, most of South America, Western Australia, the Kalahari Craton and parts of Antarctica. Cluster GU-NF (Great Unconformity—no formation) spanned most of Africa, Asia, parts of Antarctica and the São Francisco Craton (Fig. 3a). Cluster GU-F captured positive dynamic topography (Fig. 3d), mainly above whole-mantle upwelling (Supplementary Video 1). Dynamic topography was relatively stable between 900 Ma and 800 Ma, increased rapidly between 800 Ma and 720 Ma, followed by a gradual increase between 720 Ma and 600 Ma, and a rapid decrease between 600 Ma and 420 Ma (Fig. 3d). The predicted uplift would have promoted glacial erosion1,13 during the proposed Sturtian and Marinoan global glaciations (Fig. 3d). The GU-F pattern of prolonged dynamic uplift during Neoproterozoic times (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2), followed by dynamic subsidence during Cambrian times (Fig. 3d) was consistent across all mantle convection models (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3a,c,e). Cluster GU-NF captured dynamic topography on average negative throughout 920–420 Ma with gradual increase between 900 Ma and 760 Ma, a rapid decline between 760 Ma and 520 Ma, and renewed increase between 520 Ma and 420 Ma (Fig. 3d). In cluster GU-NF, Siberia and the Congo and West African cratons were in a dynamic topography low surrounded by subduction zones (Fig. 2a,c and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2).

For the period 420–0 Ma, cluster GU-HPP (Great Unconformity—high preservation potential) spanned Western Laurentia, Baltica, North China and Siberia, and cluster GU-LPP (Great Unconformity—low preservation potential) spanned Eastern Laurentia, Africa, Australia, Antarctica and India (Fig. 3b). The dynamic topography for GU-HPP, which was generally negative because of subduction (Supplementary Video 1), remained relatively stable between 420 Ma and 240 Ma, before gradually declining until 0 Ma (Fig. 3e). By contrast, in GU-LPP dynamic topography increased between 420 Ma and 240 Ma, was stable between 240 Ma and 120 Ma, then gradually declined until 0 Ma (Fig. 3e).

We derived a map highlighting the areas in which the Great Unconformity was predicted to have formed and to have a high preservation potential, which consisted of Laurentia, Baltica and northeastern North China for model M1 (Fig. 3c) and included areas around Laurentia and Baltica in all six models (Extended Data Figs. 3 and 4). We analysed the sensitivity of these results to the number of clusters (either two or three) for each period (formation 920–420 Ma, preservation from 420 Ma) from vote maps (Methods) of areas in which the Great Unconformity was predicted to exist across the six models (Extended Data Fig. 5). This confirmed that Laurentia, Baltica and North China were the main continental blocks in which the Great Unconformity was predicted to have formed and to be preserved, with northern South America emerging as a possible additional region (Extended Data Fig. 5).

The dynamic topography evolution predicted by our models was consistent with the preserved sediment flux for each continent except Africa1,14 (Fig. 4 and Methods). Predicted prolonged Precambrian uplift, followed by rapid Cambrian subsidence, generally matched increased sediment flux across the Precambrian–Cambrian boundary (Fig. 4a–e). A shift from erosion to sedimentation reflecting decreasing dynamic topography (Fig. 4) and flooded continents (Extended Data Fig. 6a) was predicted for all continents except for Eurasia and Africa, which consisted of tectonic blocks with contrasting Neoproterozoic histories. In Eurasia, dynamic uplift was predicted for Baltica and North China, and dynamic subsidence for Siberia40 (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Figs. 7d and 8b,g,l,q,v,aa). In Africa, dynamic uplift was predicted for the Kalahari Craton, and dynamic subsidence for the Congo and West African cratons (Extended Data Figs. 7e and 8e,j,o,t,y,ad) was consistent with their sedimentary record of long-lived depocentres41,42. Extensive Precambrian orogens within Africa enhanced erosion and sedimentation (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6), leading to a landscape in which negative dynamic topography did not result in increased sediment flux at the base of the Cambrian (Extended Data Fig. 6a,c,e,g).

a–e, Evolution of the preserved volume of sediment per year and per unit continental area (increasing down) (left y axis, coloured bar charts) and dynamic topography (right y axis, grey bar charts and coloured lines) for each continent averaged at time steps corresponding to the sediment preservation data1,14. Coloured solid and dotted lines represent the evolution of dynamic topography for Laurentia and continental blocks in Eurasia. f–j, Data in a–e temporally averaged for dynamic topography cycles in each continent. In each panel, the vertical dashed line represents the start of Cambrian times, and the horizontal dashed line represents the datum for dynamic topography.

The evolution of predicted Phanerozoic dynamic topography differed across continental blocks. Laurentia, Baltica and North China were characterized by sustained dynamic subsidence, which aligned with increased preserved sediment flux across North America and Eurasia (Fig. 4). Conversely, predicted renewed dynamic uplift of South America and of Australia, which would have eroded earlier unconformities11,31 and formed new ones, corresponded to decreased preserved sediment flux (Fig. 4).

Importantly, the number of dynamic topography uplift–subsidence cycles governed the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity. A single cycle of Precambrian uplift followed by Phanerozoic subsidence was the ideal scenario for forming and preserving the Great Unconformity. This scenario, which is in first-order agreement with thermochronology studies3,4,7,10,18, was predicted for Laurentia for all models except M3 (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 8a,f,k,p,v,z). Although Laurentia was in cluster GU-F for model M3 (Extended Data Fig. 2), it was not predicted to have experienced notable uplift and was subsiding above a mantle downwelling at 640 Ma (Extended Data Fig. 9). Together with a poor match of the present-day mantle structure for M3 (Extended Data Fig. 1d), this confirmed that NNR was an appropriate reference frame to model mantle flow33, but not PMAG in which lithospheric net rotation was large. Precambrian uplift was predicted for four out of six models for Baltica and North China, with marked variations in amplitude and duration between models (Extended Data Fig. 8b,g,l,q,v,aa), possibly reflecting particularly uncertain subduction history (Supplementary Discussion and Supplementary Table 1). All models predicted dynamic uplift of Baltica as it moved from the southern hemisphere to the northern hemisphere between 540 Ma and 520 Ma (Supplementary Videos 1 and 2), followed by rapid subsidence consistent with a sub-Cambrian unconformity linked to epeirogenic uplift22,43.

By contrast, most models predicted two cycles of dynamic uplift followed by dynamic subsidence for South America and Australia and long-lived dynamic subsidence followed by dynamic uplift then renewed dynamic subsidence for Africa (Fig. 4h–j and Extended Data Fig. 8c–ad), consistent with thermochronological and geochronological evidence for these regions44,45,46,47,48. The predicted dynamic uplift of South America and Australia coincided with preserved sediment flux on these continents, as expected (Fig. 4h,i and Extended Data Fig. 8c–ac). However, the dynamic uplift of Africa coincided with increased sediment preservation because Africa was positioned centrally in Gondwana (Extended Data Fig. 6b) and orogens in Antarctica and South America (Fig. 3f) restricted drainage from Africa to the oceans, leading to endorheic (inland) sedimentation49.

The solution of the presented flow models depends strongly on the tectonic reconstruction, for which the uncertainty is large and increases back in time (Supplementary Discussion and Supplementary Table 1). Testing the sensitivity of the flow model to the tectonic scenario is a challenge that could be addressed by developing alternative tectonic reconstructions with continuously closing plate polygons or by developing a different approach to predict past mantle flow.

Comparing dynamic topography cycles to preserved sediment flux confirmed Laurentia, Baltica and North China as continental blocks on which the Great Unconformity was predicted to have formed and to be preserved (Fig. 4). The Great Unconformity surface is exposed and extensively studied in Laurentia1,3,5,6,7,9,10,15,18 and in North China8,25,26,27,28, whereas it is mostly inferred to occur beneath younger sediments in Baltica19,20,21,22,23,24. This largely stems from the tectonic and geodynamic evolution of each of these continental blocks. In the considered tectonic scenario, no subduction occurred directly along the margins of Laurentia between about 930 Ma and 510 Ma, Baltica between about 750 Ma and 520 Ma, and North China between about 720 Ma and 540 Ma (Supplementary Discussion, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). Subduction beneath northeast Laurentia from approximately 470 Ma resulted in its amalgamation with Baltica into Laurussia by around 420 Ma, associated with continent-wide Cambrian transgression (Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). North China was on the periphery of Gondwana during Cambrian times with the Qinling subduction zone system at its western margin from 540 Ma (Fig. 2b, Supplementary Discussion, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). During the assembly of Pangea, collisions occurred along some margins of all three continental blocks (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6b), promoting the deformation and erosion of rocks potentially preserving the Great Unconformity, or their burial in foreland basins. The large continental area of Laurentia and limited reworking at its margins were favourable to recording the formation of the continental-scale Great Unconformity. The prominent exposure of the Great Unconformity in the Grand Canyon15,16,17 has been linked to the Laramide uplift event from Farallon flat-slab subduction and subsequent Colorado River incision50,51. Repeated orogeny along the eastern margin of Baltica (Fig. 3f) could explain why the Great Unconformity is generally inferred to occur at depth on that smaller continental block. Early Cretaceous lithospheric delamination52 could explain the exposure of the Great Unconformity in North China, which is unexpected given its comparatively small area and four episodes of orogenesis between about 500 Ma and 200 Ma (Fig. 3f).

Our models predict changes in dynamic topography that when averaged in time and space by k-means clustering occur over approximately 20 Myr and about 5,000 km, suggesting that the motion of continents over the convecting mantle provided the large-scale geodynamic environments that favoured the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity in Laurentia, Baltica and North China. The geologic record of uplift4,5,6,7,10,53 and subsidence4,5,6,7,9,10,20 indicates that the timing of erosion and deposition54 varied between locations, which probably reflects the effect of processes, such as tectonic deformation, elastic flexure or shorter wavelength dynamic topography, that would affect relative sea level over shorter spatial and temporal scales.

The amplitude of long-wavelength dynamic topography is thought to be about a tenth of the amplitude of tectonic topography37, and continental tilting would not result in the formation of slopes that would lead to sufficient fluvial erosion to explain the magnitude of denudation associated with the Great Unconformity1,4,7. We propose that sustained positive dynamic topography throughout Cryogenian times (Fig. 3d) would have resulted in substantial erosion because glacial erosion rates exceed fluvial erosion rates by an order of magnitude and can operate at lower elevations13. The rarity of extensive unconformities in the history of Earth could be due to the very long timescale (>900 Myr) of the proposed continental-scale uplift and subsidence to form such an unconformity, combined with rare extensive glaciations and decreasing preservation potential back in geological time.

Our models explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved in North America and show that it is a first-order surface expression of deep geodynamic processes that transformed global landscapes and sediment fluxes. In turn, these landscape dynamics would have altered seawater chemistry and catalysed the Cambrian explosion of life2. Future work could investigate the effects of continental-scale dynamic uplift and subsidence on erosion, sedimentation, seawater chemistry and their consequences for the diversification of life forms.

Macrostrat is an open, relational geospatial database that enables large-scale, quantitative analysis of 33,903 lithologically and chronologically defined rock units across 1,474 regions in the Americas, New Zealand and the deep sea55.

We accessed lithostratigraphic data from the Macrostrat (https://macrostrat.org/api/units/?lith_class=sedimentary&lith_type=metasedimentary) database through theAPI (v.2). We downloaded sedimentary units and associated stratigraphic columns as GeoJSON files in June 2025. We created a map of transgressive sequences and erosional remnants across North America and northern South America (Fig. 1) spanning late Neoproterozoic to early Ordovician times.

We used the code CitcomS57 to model mantle convection for a billion years (1,000–0 Ma). In CitcomS, the mantle structure is represented with finite-element nodes in 3D spherical geometry. We considered six model cases (Extended Data Table 1), three of which have been presented in previous work (M4 was MF in ref. 58; M5 was C3 in ref. 59, C20 in ref. 33 and C3 in ref. 60; and M6 was C1 in ref. 59).

We discretized the mantle into about 13 million nodes (129 × 129 × 65 × 12), with radial mesh refinements at the surface (about 50 × 50 × 15 km) and core–mantle boundary (CMB; about 28 × 28 × 27 km) and relatively lower resolution in the mid-mantle (approximately 40 × 40 × 100 km). We reconstructed mantle flow in a modified version of CitcomS57,61 in which plate kinematics and the thermal structure of the oceanic lithosphere and subducting slabs down to 350 km depth were derived from tectonic reconstructions62 with continuously closing plate polygons63 and imposed as time-dependent boundary conditions in 1 million-year increments. We used the extended Boussinesq approximation that assumed the mantle to be an incompressible fluid to account for viscous dissipation, internal heating, depth-dependent thermal expansion coefficient and an adiabatic temperature gradient64.

For initial boundary conditions and time-progressive model simulation, we created a lithospheric thermal structure from reconstructed seafloor ages and half-space cooling with a maximum seafloor age set as 80 Myr to obtain a maximum thickness of oceanic lithosphere consistent with observations for the present day. We used the method in ref. 65 to reconstruct synthetic seafloor ages, whereas the continental lithosphere adopted simplified tectonothermal ages from ref. 66. The global thermal regime of continental lithosphere and subducting slabs, reconstructed using seafloor ages and location of subduction zones61, was imposed in the flow models in increments of 1 million years.

The initial conditions included an adiabatic temperature profile between two boundary layers: the lithosphere at the surface, and a 225 km thick laterally uniform basal layer containing a 113 km thick layer with excess density. The density contrast δρb between the basal layer and the ambient mantle was defined by the buoyancy ratio \(B=\frac{{\rm{\delta }}{\rho }_{{\rm{b}}}}{\rho \alpha \Delta T}\) where ΔT = 4,300 K was the temperature change across mantle for M1–M3 (ΔT = 3,600 K for M4 and ΔT = 2,800 K for M5 and M6), ρ = 5,546 kg m−3 was the average density67 and α = 1.32 × 10−5 K−1 was thermal expansivity68 in the 100 km layer above the CMB. The initial condition consisted of slabs inserted down to 1,000 km depth for models M1–M4 (1,200 km for models M5 and 550 km for M6) with dip angles of 45° dip down to 425 km depth and 90° descent below. To incorporate the advective thickening of more viscous lower mantle, lower mantle slabs were twice as thick as upper mantle slabs in the initial condition. Models were initialized with differing warm-up phases lasting 250 Myr for models M1 and M4, 200 Myr for models M6 and 0 Myr for other models (Extended Data Table 1) using the 1 Ga configuration for tectonic velocities, subduction zone positions and lithospheric age. Boundary conditions were isothermal at the surface and at the CMB, imposed plate kinematics (velocities) at the surface and a free-slip kinematic condition at the CMB.

The convective vigour in models was governed by the Rayleigh number \({\rm{R}}{\rm{a}}=\frac{{\alpha }_{0}\rho g\Delta T{h}_{{\rm{M}}}^{3}}{\kappa {\eta }_{0}}\), where α0 = 3 × 10−5 K−1 was the coefficient of thermal expansion at the surface, ρ = 4,000 kg m−3 was the density, g = 9.81 m s−2 was the gravitational acceleration, hM = 2,867 km was the thickness of the mantle, κ = 1 × 10−6 m2 s−1 was the thermal diffusivity, η0 = 1 × 1021 Pa s was the reference viscosity. The subscript ‘0’ indicated reference values. The coefficient of thermal expansion was depth-dependent, decreasing by a factor of about 2 over the thickness of the mantle (see refs. 68,69). Based on these values, we obtained Ra = 1.2 × 108 for M1–M3. The Rayleigh number was varied across model cases (Extended Data Table 1).

Likewise, the dissipation number governed heat dissipation generated by shear heating. It was given by \({\rm{D}}{\rm{i}}=\frac{{\alpha }_{0}g{h}_{{\rm{M}}}}{{C}_{p}}\), where 2867 Cp = 1,200 J kg−1 K−1 was the heat capacity. The total rate of internal heating was equal to 33.6 TW, accounting for contributions from both radioactive decay (about 9–17 TW; ref. 70) and primordial heat dissipated through secular cooling of the interior of Earth (around 8–29 TW; ref. 70).

Depth-, composition-, temperature- and pressure-dependent viscosity was computed as

The depth-dependent viscosity pre-factor η(r) was equal to 2 × 1019 Pa s above 160 km depth and between 310 km and 660 km depth (upper mantle), to 6 × 1017 Pa s in the asthenosphere between 60 km and 310 km depth for models M1–M3 (2 × 1018 Pa s for models M4–M6), and 6 × 1020 Pa s in the lower mantle below 660 km depth for models M1–M3 (2 × 1020 Pa s for models M4–M6; Extended Data Table 1). The compositional viscosity pre-factors ηC were equal to 1 for ambient mantle, to 100 for continental lithosphere (modelled as in ref. 66), and to 10 for the basal layer. The term r was the radius, Rc = 3,504 km was the radius of the core, Eη = 284 kJ mol−1 was the activation energy, Zη = 2.1 × 10−6 m3 mol−1 was the activation volume, Ru = 8.31 J mol−1 K−1 was the universal gas constant, T was the dimensional temperature, Toff = 694 K was a temperature offset and TCMB = 4,300 K was the temperature at the core–mantle boundary. The viscosity structure, defined by the viscosity pre-factors, activation volume, activation energy and temperature offset produced viscosity variations varying over three orders of magnitude across the model33. Although these contrasts were smaller than expected for the solid Earth71, these lateral viscosity variations could be resolved at a spatial resolution that allows time-dependent mantle flow to be computed using up to about 15,000 CPU hours per 100 million years on supercomputer Gadi.

We derived boundary conditions from the global tectonic reconstructions in ref. 62 (which merges with tectonic reconstructions in refs. 72,73,74,75), which was the only tectonic reconstruction extending back to 1 billion years ago with continuously closing plate polygons that are necessary in models based on the approach in ref. 61. We considered two reference frames for the tectonic reconstruction in ref. 62: the original palaeomagnetic reference frame (PMAG, model M3) and a no-net-rotation reference frame (NNR), which was suitable to model mantle convection33,76. We analysed model results, including dynamic topography, mantle temperature and composition fields in increments of 20 million years.

We computed air-loaded dynamic topography at the surface of Earth as \(h=\frac{{\sigma }_{\mathrm{rr}}}{\Delta \rho g}\), where g = 9.81 m s−2 was the acceleration of gravity and Δρ was the difference in densities between air (ρA = 0 kg m−3) and the shallow upper mantle (ρUM = 3,320 kg m−3). We considered free-slip boundary conditions, contributions from sources of buoyancy deeper than 350 km depth, and lateral viscosity variations deeper than 350 km depth.

As in refs. 32,33,77, we first classified the present-day lower mantle structure as mapped by 10 independent S-wave tomographic models78,79,80,81,82,83,84,85,86,87 and predicted by six mantle flow models (M1–M6). To achieve this, we generated 196,965 evenly spaced points (about 0.45°) on the surface and sampled mantle temperature (seismic velocity) approximately every 58 km between 1,000 km and 2,800 km depths. We then used k-means88 clustering to group these points into user-specified k clusters such that the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS), that is, the squared Euclidean distances between points and the centroid of the group was minimized.

As in previous studies32,33, we examined model success by computing three metrics (Extended Data Fig. 1): (1) the predicted fractional area fa of the surface of Earth covered by clusters for hot BLOBSs (for mantle flow models) and slow LLSVPs (for tomographic models), (2) the global accuracy (\(\overline{\mathrm{Acc}}\)), which was a measure of the spatial match between the present-day mantle structure (clusters) predicted by mantle convection models and that averaged across 10 independent tomographic models given by \(\overline{\mathrm{Acc}}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{TN}}{A}\), where TP was the area of true positives representing spatial match between hot BLOBSs and LLSVPs, TN the area of the true negatives measuring the spatial extent of cold basal mantle structure and high seismic velocity profiles and A was the total surface area of Earth. For each model, the mean accuracy \(\overline{\mathrm{Acc}}\) represented the average across 10 tomographic models, whereas for each tomographic model, \(\overline{\mathrm{Acc}}\) was computed as an average across the nine independent tomographic models; and (3) the time-averaged median angular distance \(\widetilde{\theta }\) between reconstructed volcanic eruption locations (LIPs and kimberlites as in ref. 33) from 320 Ma and the edge of hot BLOBSs. The distance was taken as zero for eruption locations above a BLOBS or LLSVP. Smaller distances indicated a close spatial match between BLOBSs or LLSVPs and volcanic eruptions, which was thought to be favourable32,33,89. Mantle flow models were deemed to perform better if all three metrics were within the range or close to the range for tomographic models (Extended Data Fig. 1, grey areas).

We generated a set of evenly spaced (about 0.45°) points entirely covering present-day continents. We extracted dynamic topography at the reconstructed location of these points in 20 Myr intervals and rotated the results back into the present-day plate configuration. We used the continental blocks that continuously existed from 920 Ma to mask data for all other times so that the considered locations existed for all considered times. We used k-means clustering88 as in ref. 90 to classify geographic regions that share a similar evolution of predicted dynamic topography.

We used the silhouette91 score, Davies–Bouldin index92 (DBI) and elbow method93to determine the appropriate number of clusters to consider (Supplementary Fig. 1). The silhouette score measured how similar a point was to its own cluster compared with other clusters. It combined intra-cluster cohesion and inter-cluster separation. Silhouette scores ranged from −1 to 1, with larger values indicating better-defined clusters. The DBI evaluated intra-cluster similarity and inter-cluster differences based on intra-cluster dispersion and inter-cluster distance. Lower scores indicated better clustering. It was computationally efficient but assumed compact, spherical clusters, making it less reliable for irregular shapes. The heuristic elbow method consisted of plotting the number of clusters (k) against the clustering cost (for example, WCSS) and identifying the ‘elbow’ point, at which the rate of improvement (decrease in WCSS) decreased sharply, suggesting the most appropriate k.

We identified the ideal number of clusters for all six model cases for both the Great Unconformity formation (920–420 Ma) and preservation (420–0 Ma) periods to be equal to either two or three (Supplementary Fig. 1). We produced cluster maps for each model case and each cluster combination (either two or three) and combined them in maps indicating model agreement with a score between zero and six out of six models. These ‘vote’ maps highlighted regions showing both formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity across model and cluster combinations (Extended Data Fig. 5).

We obtained the preserved sediment flux (sediment volume divided by time) from Neoproterozoic times (1.6 Ga) to the present for North America, South America, Africa, Eurasia and Australia from ref. 1. For the period 920–0 Ma, we scaled sediment flux by the present-day area of each considered continent as in ref. 1. We averaged continental dynamic topography for each continental block that continuously existed between 920 Ma and 0 Ma (Extended Data Fig. 8a) using the time periods at which sediment volume data were defined (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8).

To focus on long-term, long-wavelength processes, we filtered the preserved sediment data using time windows that corresponded to the periods of dynamic uplift and dynamic subsidence predicted for each continent. We then averaged the preserved sediment volume to represent the sediment accumulation associated with each phase of dynamic topography (Fig. 4f–j).

The subduction convergence rates at trench segments were computed using plate-kinematic workflow of GPlately (v.2.0.0), built atop PyGPlates94, a Python interface for GPlates95 and PlateTectonicTools. The process consisted of resolving the topological plate model and extracting subduction zones from the network of dynamic plate boundaries reconstructed at a specified age using the NNR model. Each subduction zone was then tessellated, that is, discretized into a series of evenly spaced points using the ‘tessellation_subduction_zone’ module in GPlately. At each tessellated point, subduction convergence rate, obliquity and trench migration rate were calculated from the relative motion of the down-going and overriding plates at each reconstruction time step. Negative convergence-rate values, which indicated infrequent inconsistencies in the model with divergence occurring at a convergent boundary72, were set to zero before computing the range of convergence rates for each subduction zone listed in Supplementary Table 1.

#1421. Now will the FA put their money where their mouth is? England chiefs and UEFA must decide whether to back rival Japanese bid to FIFA president Gianni Infantino after slamming World Cup controversial sell-off plan

Published: 08:23 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 11:00 EDT, 5 November 2026

The FA and UEFA face a dilemma over whether to support a bid to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency after honorary Japanese FA president Kohzo Tashima announced his decision to stand.

Alongside the FA, UEFA have spearheaded opposition to Infantino following the collapse of his botched deal to sell stakes in the World Cup.

However, despite declaring Infantino 'has lost the confidence of UEFA' and threatening to boycott the World Cup, the European governing body have so far failed to come up with a candidate to challenge him at the March election in Rabat.

UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin decided against a run for the FIFA presidency, opting instead to focus on securing another term at the top of European football.

At a meeting of the FA Council last month FA chair Debbie Hewitt demanded answers over the World Cup sell-off plan - and decision to suspend the ban of US striker Folarin Balogun after pressure from Donald Trump. She said: 'The man has to answer those questions, and if he doesn't answer those questions, no, he's not fit to be FIFA president, and that was what was shared in the meeting.'

But there is a growing feeling that a European candidate would struggle to secure sufficient support from the rest of the world, while Infantino believes he already has enough votes to secure re-election, making it difficult to find a credible challenger.

Japanese FA president Kohzo Tashima has announced a decision to stand for FIFA presidency

Tashima will run against the controversial current president Gianni Infantino (left)

That said, FIFA Council member and Japanese FA bigwig Tashima could split the Asian vote and is well respected in Europe.

With Tashima - the first candidate to secure the backing of a national association - declaring his intention to run, pressure is now mounting on the FA and UEFA to either support his bid or put forward a candidate of their own, having called for Infantino to step down.

It follows former Tottenham and Switzerland footballer Ramon Vega making a public leadership bid on Wednesday, though it is unclear whether he could obtain the backing of enough national associations.

Candidates require the support of five football associations to run for the presidency and must pass eligibility checks by November 18.

Tashima is the first candidate with a realistic chance to announce an intention to run before the November 18 deadline, where the support of five national associations is required.

Speaking to Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon, Tashima said: ‘I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association.

‘It’s not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world.’

#1420. Everton Women Unwrap New Partnership With Nestlé Confectionery

Everton Women has announced a new multi-year partnership with Nestlé Confectionery, bringing one of the world's most recognisable food and beverage companies into the Club's growing portfolio of commercial partners.

The agreement will see Nestlé Confectionery become the 'Official Chocolate and Grab Bag Sweet Partner of Everton Women' and an 'Official Supplier of Hill Dickinson Stadium', with household favourites including KitKat, Smarties, Rowntree's, Aero, Lion, Yorkie, Milkybar and Quality Street set to feature across both venues.

At Goodison Park, Nestlé Confectionery will have a prominent presence through pitchside LED advertising, big-screen exposure and matchday activations designed to engage supporters, alongside opportunities to showcase its products at food kiosks and points of sale.

Supporters and visitors to Hill Dickinson Stadium will also be able to enjoy Nestlé Confectionery's popular range of products, extending the brand's presence across both of Everton's iconic stadiums.

The agreement represents Everton Women's second dedicated commercial partnership, following last year's deal with GGM Gastro, with further Everton Women's-focused partnerships set to be announced.

The growing interest from major businesses reflects the opportunities being created around Everton Women, with the team's move to Goodison Park offering prospective partners a unique combination of footballing heritage, an iconic stadium and access to new audiences as the women's game continues to develop.

Andrew Middleton, President of Business Operations at Everton, said:  “We are delighted to welcome Nestlé Confectionery as a partner of Everton Women and an Official Supplier of Hill Dickinson Stadium.

“Like Everton, Nestlé’s brands have been part of family life for generations, making this a natural fit for our supporters and matchday experience. Together, we will create engaging moments across both venues and bring these iconic products closer to our audiences.

“This partnership is another important step in Everton Women’s continued growth, and we look forward to working with Nestlé to bring it to life.”

Gail Stove, OOH Confectionery Lead for Nestlé UK & Ireland, said: "Nestlé Confectionery is excited to be an Official Partner of Everton Women and Official Supplier of Hill Dickinson Stadium.

"We can’t wait to share our beloved brands with visitors at these brilliant venues.

“Working collaboratively with Everton Football Club, we’ll bring the No.1 confectionery single within the leisure channel, KitKat® 4 Finger, along with other iconic Nestlé Confectionery brands for everyone to enjoy.”

Further details of Nestlé Confectionery's planned matchday activations and opportunities for Everton supporters to engage with its brands will be announced in the coming months.

#1419. Spurs finally score... but still lose

They scored. Would you believe it? Tottenham Hotspur, the team with more zeroes than an England Ashes batting collapse, found the back of the net but still frustration persists for Roberto De Zerbi.

It could have been something different. The sight of the Italian dashing down the touchline in hailstones, grabbing his head in disbelief in the final seconds, showed this was not a straightforward tale of misery but, ultimately, the misery endures.

“I think this is five or six games we have been for sure not lucky,” De Zerbi lamented, but sympathy did not extend too far. Liverpool deservedly moved into the next round of the Carabao Cup, the gloss on Andoni Iraola’s most enjoyable night provided by Dominik Szoboszlai’s goal-of-the-season contender.

THAT'S MAGNIFICENT! 💥🔴Outrageous strike from Dominik Szoboszlai 👏👏👏 pic.twitter.com/meQ7nilsz6

Liverpool were abject against Fulham on Saturday but with 10 changes to the starting line-up, infused with the exuberance of novices Rio Ngumoha and the terrific Lewis Koumas, Iraola’s team were invigorated and only a lapse of concentration enabled Tottenham to make a fist of it.

Yes, they went down swinging, as their noisy fans demanded. But carelessness cannot be excused and while De Zerbi complained about bad luck, a bad miss from Lucas Bergvall in the 10th minute was the fork in the road for the tie. Tottenham stalled and Liverpool never looked back.

“We have to shoot more times and we have to shoot better,” De Zerbi harrumphed. “We have to finish better the clear situations. We are sorry for the result, disappointed and frustrated. I think it was unfair but we have to be stronger in these unlucky moments.”

Rather than fizzing his drive into the net, Bergvall succeeded only in firing straight at Giorgi Mamardashvili, when he had the whole target in front of him. It was, in all fairness, a brilliant save but he should never have been allowed to make it.

Big save from Giorgi Mamardashvili! 💪Lucas Bergvall is denied by the Liverpool goalkeeper. pic.twitter.com/fKUbfGLMku

The miss changed the atmosphere, as suddenly Liverpool grasped the need to be competitive. At the heart of it all were Ngumoha, James McConnell, Trey Nyoni and Koumas, the last-named a nuisance to Tottenham’s defenders in the way a wasp is to picnickers on a summer’s afternoon.

For all the money that has been lavished by this club over the past 14 months, the one thing that the locals buy into more than anything is the basics done properly: hard work, tackling, a refusal to take second best. Iraola did not want Koumas to go anywhere this summer and it was obvious why.

“I see him training every day,” Iraola said. “He knows very clearly what he needs to do, what the team needs. And also the energy he shows is contagious for the rest. When you see the runs up front, giving everything, you are kind of forced to go behind and use the same intensity levels.”

Simple tenacity enabled Liverpool to get back on an even keel and laid the foundation for them to take the lead. It was a terrific goal, started with a raking pass from Joe Gomez that Cody Gakpo controlled instantly on his chest before scuttling inside and inviting Ngumoha to charge forward.

Whether it was the winger or Destiny Udogie, who was sliding to make a challenge, that ended up playing the ball to Alexis Mac Allister is immaterial, all that mattered is that the Argentine effortlessly placed his shot into the top corner, leaving Martin Dubravka planted and helpless.

Pick that out!! 🇦🇷Alexis Mac Allister hits a beauty into the roof of the net 🔴 pic.twitter.com/G7OT27CA8P

Is Mac Allister playing with a point to prove? Possibly, given his comments about not being offered a new contract last week. Will Iraola be bothered? Not in the slightest. All he wants is top players at the top of their game and Mac Allister is climbing towards the levels he showed two years ago.

What De Zerbi would do to have a player in such form, but Tottenham are a skittish bunch, not the type of team who respond well in the face of adversity and their head coach, dressed in black with his oversized white trainers, regularly shook his head in exasperation.

His mood was not helped just before the interval, when Mohammed Kudus blasted over from eight yards following a zipped-in cross from Udogie, but he would not have called it truthfully if he had suggested Tottenham deserved parity at that stage. Soon Liverpool’s advantage would be doubled.

The buffer they sought arrived in the 54th minute and, again, it was another genuinely attractive goal, with possession being kept until it sped up when Ngumoha scurried forward, found Milos Kerkez, who played it to Mac Allister, who in turn gave Gakpo the opening he craved.

His touch was excellent, his finish was even better and away in the distance Iraola rattled his fists in delight. That is two goals and four assists to start the campaign for the Dutchman and yet Liverpool were ready to sell him to Manchester City two weeks ago. What on earth were they thinking?

Ruthless!! 🔥Cody Gakpo doubles Liverpool's lead against Spurs 🔴 pic.twitter.com/qlaaynMuwM

From that point, it seemed inconceivable that Liverpool would finish living on their nerves, but De Zerbi’s decision to introduce Andy Robertson – given a hero’s reception on his first return to Anfield – and Mateus Fernandes wrestled back some impetus. There was also a significant helping hand.

Unsurprisingly, Andy Robertson gets a great reception from the Liverpool fans on his return to Anfield 👏 pic.twitter.com/uNM6A00k5F

Mamardashvili had made some important saves, including one from Kudus that he celebrated on his own, but he is vulnerable at set-pieces and Fernandes’s looping corner gave Conor Gallagher the easiest headed opportunity in three years to change the dynamic.

Spurs have scored! ⚪️Conor Gallagher brings Roberto De Zerbi's side back into the game! pic.twitter.com/52zSCqClw4

“We were under pressure at the end, but I don’t think we were nervous,” Gakpo said.

He was right. Try as they might, Spurs could not quite get the opening they needed and as they chased in vain, Szoboszlai administered the final blow in mesmerising fashion, thrashing a bouncing ball into the Kop net from 30 yards. And as De Zerbi realised in the sodden conditions, with Tottenham it never rains. It only pours.

"A Steven Gerrard type of strike" 😍Jamie Redknapp and Conor Coady analyse Dominik Szoboszlai's wondergoal 🪄 pic.twitter.com/h9QTuP8lZc

🗣️ "The young players give us energy" 💪Andoni Iraola is very pleased with the way the Liverpool youngsters played after beating Spurs 3-1 at Anfield 👏#ITVFootball | @Carabao_Cup | @markpougatch | @Robbie9Fowler pic.twitter.com/bHjOrmccH2

🗣️"Szoboszlai scores A LOT OF BANGERS"😂Needless to say Cody Gakpo was really impressed with Dominik Szoboszlai's goal for Liverpool 👏#ITVFootball | @LFC | @Carabao_Cup | @gabrielclarke05 pic.twitter.com/O3bs6Y9M2p

"They've done themselves proud!" 👏Conor Coady on Lewis Koumas performance for Liverpool 🔥 pic.twitter.com/3JGkuY7Eye

"You can never take it for granted!"Cody Gakpo and Lewis Koumas on Liverpool's confident win over Spurs in the third round of the Carabao Cup 👏 pic.twitter.com/mGHo8FZGeE

"I focus quite a lot on them, sometimes I get angry but it's part of me wanting them to succeed" 🔴"They deserve this, they know what the club means" Alexis Mac Allister was full of praise for Liverpool's youngsters after their 3-1 win over Spurs 👏#ITVFootball pic.twitter.com/RdEHZrv4Qy

“From Tottenham’s point of view, there were positives. They had a sharpness to their game. [Lucas] Bergvall did well. There is lots to look forward to for the weekend. It was a better performance. On another day, they could have had two or three goals. Liverpool just had enough.”

Peterborough 3 Barnsley 3 (Peterborough won 7-6 on penalties)West Ham 2 Fulham 3Ipswich 2 Arsenal 4Liverpool 3 Tottenham 1Reading 1 Brentford 2

Moments after the ball thumped into the back of the net:

Possession: Liverpool 44%-56% TottenhamShots: 12-17Shots on target: 5-6Corners: 5-9Touches in opposition box: 22-27

Andrew Robertson received a great reception from the Anfield crowd whilst warming up, when he came on and now at full-time. He catches up with old teammates as he heads off in the pouring rain, applauding the Liverpool fans.

There is the final whistle at Anfield and Liverpool book their place in the fourth round of the League Cup courtesy of a 3-1 win over Tottenham. Andoni Iraola’s side scored three stunning goals to seal their progression.

Mamardashvili does well to save from a deflection, like he did a few minutes ago. Mamardashvili did not cover himself in glory for Tottenham’s goal but has made some great saves tonight.

Oh my word! The Hungarian loves a screamer and this is another to add to the list. It is similar to a goal Suarez scored at The Kop End against Norwich a number of years ago. Szoboszlai chests it down and from nearly 30 yards out smashes across the ball. The ball flies into to the top corner, always going away from Dubravka, and Szoboszlai celebrates in front of The Kop. A quite incredible goal.

THAT'S MAGNIFICENT! 💥🔴Outrageous strike from Dominik Szoboszlai 👏👏👏 pic.twitter.com/meQ7nilsz6

There will be four added minutes at Anfield.

Savio has an effort from the right side of the box but drags his shot wide of the far post.

Liverpool counter with Mamardashvili’s long ball forward for Isak, who gets the better of Gray on the left side of the box. Isak gets his shot away and the ball appeared to hit Tosin’s arm but the penalty is not given. Replays show it did hit Tosin’s arm and he is lucky there is not VAR tonight as that could well have been overturned.

Solanke is on for Tottenham in place of Tel as the visitors have a corner out on the right. Tottenham take it short before the delivery is swung in and headed away by Gakpo as the rain comes thrashing down again at Anfield.

Tottenham keep it alive and Marmoush has an effort from the left side of the box. It deflects off Araujo and Mamardashvili makes a stunning save.

Szoboszlai should bury a guilt-edge chance inside the Tottenham penalty area but his effort is saved. There was a suspicion of offside against Szoboszlai but the flag did not go up. Szoboszlai was being played onside by quite some way by Gray so a huge missed opportunity.

That is superb one-vs-one defending from Jacquet. The ball is played down the left channel but Jacquet gets the better of Marmoush.

Into the final 10 minutes we go at Anfield.

Liverpool are under pressure at the moment as Tottenham attack the Anfield Road End, where the travelling Spurs supporters are housed. Mamardashvili is again unconvincing when dealing with a corner into the box.

Double change for Tottenham as Savio and Maddison replace Kudus and Gallagher.

That is a stupid challenge from Kerkez, who is booked for a silly foul on Gallagher. Kerkez was asking for a booking for that challenge and referee Andy Madley obliges.

Change for Liverpool as Barcola replaces Ngumoha.

The visitors take advantage of very poor keeping from Mamardashvili. Fernandes’ delivery should be dealt with by Mamardashvili but the Georgian keeper flaps at empty air. It comes to Gallagher, who has a simple header from just a few yards out. A lifeline for Tottenham, who have their first goal this season against Premier League opposition.

Spurs have scored! ⚪️Conor Gallagher brings Roberto De Zerbi's side back into the game! pic.twitter.com/52zSCqClw4

Tottenham have had some decent chances tonight. The latest comes for Gallagher just inside the Liverpool box but his effort takes a deflection off Kerkez and goes behind for a corner...

That is a crucial challenge from Kerkez inside his own box. Marmoush looked like he was going to have a great opportunity from 10 yards out in the centre of Liverpool’s penalty area but Kerkez intervenes with a superbly-timed challenge to deny the Egyptian.

Double change for Liverpool as Szoboszlai and Gravenberch replace Nyoni and McConnell in the centre of Liverpool’s midfield.

Mamardashvili makes an important save. Marmoush carries the ball a long way down Tottenham’s left before cutting inside. As he gets to the Liverpool box, he plays the ball across to his right to find Kudus, whose first-time effort is saved well by Mamardashvili down to his left.

Robertson is going to come on for Tottenham against his former side and receives a great reception from the Liverpool fans, similarly to the reception Ray Clemence received all those years ago:

Legendary goalkeeper, Ray Clemence would've turned 78 today ❤️Not many former players get a reception as good as this when they come back to Anfield, he was a true Liverpool great 🙌 pic.twitter.com/NLH3nZUJjd

Unsurprisingly, Andy Robertson gets a great reception from the Liverpool fans on his return to Anfield 👏 pic.twitter.com/uNM6A00k5F

Tosin decides to shoot from range but drags his effort wide of Mamardashvili’s right post.

The home side double their lead at The Kop end. Kerkez perhaps should shoot from the edge of the box but instead lays it back to Mac Allister. The Argentine then plays it to his left to find Gakpo, who cuts inside onto his right and fires into the far corner. This now his tenth goal in 13 League Cup appearances.

Ruthless!! 🔥Cody Gakpo doubles Liverpool's lead against Spurs 🔴 pic.twitter.com/qlaaynMuwM

No chances to speak of in the early stages of this second half.

We are back under way at Anfield. Liverpool have made a change at the break with Jacquet coming on for Gomez. This was Gomez’s first game back after injury.

Peterborough 2 Barnsley 2 (72’)West Ham 2 Fulham 2 (54’)Ipswich 0 Arsenal 2 HTLiverpool 1 Tottenham 0 HTReading 0 Brentford 2 HT

Possession: Liverpool 47%-53% TottenhamShots: 6-6Shots on target: 2-1Corners: 3-2Touches in opposition box: 10-8

Tottenham did have two big chances through Bergvall and Kudus and there are arguments to say both of them should have scored.

Mac Allister takes but his effort is off target. That is indeed the final moment of the half and Liverpool take a 1-0 lead into the break courtesy of that fine Mac Allister strike.

We are past the two initial minutes added on but that is because of the delay when Senesi was given a talking-to moments ago. That allows Liverpool to win a free-kick not far outside the Tottenham box and Bentancur is booked for the foul on Gakpo.

This will be the final moment of the half.

Senesi absolutely clatters into McConnell but somehow escapes without a booking. There have been a number of soft yellows in this first yet one of the most blatant yellows is not given as a booking.

There will be two added minutes at the end of this first half.

Marmoush is the first Tottenham player booked tonight for a foul on McConnell and that feels on the harsh side. Definitely a foul but was it a yellow?

That is a dreadful decision from referee Andy Madley. Frimpong gets the better of Tel in a contest down Tottenham’s left, with the former outmuscling the latter. Not only is Frimpong penalised, he is booked.

Mac Allister spurns a glorious chance to get his and Liverpool’s second of the night. Tottenham again risk it at the back and lose it. McConnell then feeds a pass into the box to pick out the run of Koumas, who squares it for Mac Allister. The Argentine cannot get his feet sorted in time and wastes the opportunity from eight yards out.

Liverpool want a penalty. Tottenham give it away cheaply inside their own box and McConnell goes down under a challenge from Senesi, who was the one who gave it away. It was a clumsy challenge from Senesi and if VAR was in action tonight it would have been interesting to see what they would have done with that as Senesi did barge into the back of McConnell.

Araujo is then booked for pulling Marmoush back.

There is no way Tottenham’s goal drought will last in perpetuity but they have missed two fabulous chances so far and you wonder what impact that will have on their confidence. At least one Tottenham player is being feted: Andy Robertson, who has just jogged down the touchline at Anfield in a different kit for the first time in nine years. He tried not to acknowledge the singing of his name too much but you could see it meant something to him.

The home fans serenade their former player Robertson as the now Tottenham left-back goes out to warm up.

That is a big chance for Kudus to equalise on the counter. Tottenham break from deep inside their own half and charge down their left. Bergvall waits for Udogie to come on the overlap before playing the pass. From the left side of the box, Udogie crosses for Kudus, who gets across the front of Kerkez. Kudus should probably score but lifts his effort over the bar from just six yards out.

What a goal......that would of been! 🫢Kudus fires over what would of been a sensational move from Spurs#ITVFootball | @Carabao_Cup pic.twitter.com/a1TPzKyJlP

Gomez gives the ball away cheaply inside his own half before McConnell is penalised for a foul on Marmoush. Will Tottenham cross it or take the shot on from around 25 yards out? The answer is the latter and Marmoush goes for goal but misses the target.

That was a chance for Udogie. Senesi clips in a lovely ball over the top in behind to pick out the run from left-back of Udogie, who tries to chest it down but cannot keep it under control. Had he done so, it would have been a great chance.

The way Alexis Mac Allister has played this past fortnight, anyone would think he is trying to secure himself a new contract. All cynicism aside, that was a quite beautiful goal and attention must be drawn to Cody Gakpo’s involvement: he took a pass on his chest from Joe Gomez before opening up the pitch. We will say it again: the idea of selling Gakpo in the last window was madness.

He scored a stunner nearly a week ago against Atletico Madrid here in the Champions League and he adds another storming strike to his repertoire. The ball finds kindly to Mac Allister on the edge of the box after Udogie tackled Ngumoha and the Argentine finds the top corner with a first-time finish.

Pick that out!! 🇦🇷Alexis Mac Allister hits a beauty into the roof of the net 🔴 pic.twitter.com/G7OT27CA8P

Koumas comes close to putting Liverpool in front with their first real chance of the game. Ngumoha slides a clinical pass into the box to pick out the run in behind of Koumas, who gets the better of Senesi. Koumas takes a great first touch before getting his shot away but is denied by Dubravka. Both goalkeepers have now been forced into good saves early doors.

Close for Lewis Koumas!The Liverpool youngster is denied by Martin Dubravka after some brilliant play by Rio Ngumoha 🪄 pic.twitter.com/YNC8QEAGGG

Given their team has been bang average this season, the huge number of travelling Spurs fans are making a magnificent noise. They could have celebrated a long-overdue goal had it not been for a magnificent save by Giorgi Mamardashvili. The Georgian needed to make it from Lucas Bergvall, as a minute beforehand he dithered while Joe Gomez was shepherding a ball back to him and those on the Kop lost their minds. It’s tense amongst Liverpool supporters. You wonder how it changes.

That is a fantastic save from Mamardashvili. Gallagher plays the ball to Udogie on the left side of the box and the latter squares it to Bergvall in the centre of the box. Bergvall is no more than eight yards out and must think he is going to score but Mamardashvili makes a great save to deny the Swede. Should Bergvall have given Mamardashvili the chance to save it? Maybe not.

Big save from Giorgi Mamardashvili! 💪Lucas Bergvall is denied by the Liverpool goalkeeper. pic.twitter.com/fKUbfGLMku

Tottenham are dominating possession thus far, with a lot of the game being played in Liverpool’s half at the moment.

The heavens have well and truly opened at Anfield, with the rain heaving down.

Tottenham win a corner off Gomez out on the right. Kudus clips in an inswinger that Araujo heads away.

Gakpo is starting out on the left for Liverpool tonight, with Ngumoha on the right and Koumas leading the line down the centre. Gakpo was linked with a move to Tottenham and Manchester City over the summer but stayed at Liverpool.

Tottenham have a free-kick not far outside the Liverpool penalty area on the right as Kerkez is penalised for blocking Gallagher’s cross with his arm. Kudus’ delivery is headed away by Araujo.

Kudus keeps it alive and sends in another cross that ends up in Mamardashvili’s arms.

We are under way at Anfield, with a place in the fourth round at stake.

A reminder, there is no extra time so it the game is all square after 90 minutes we will go straight to penalties. Also, there is no VAR tonight.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are moments away from kick-off at Anfield. In Virgil van Dijk’s absence, Joe Gomez captains Liverpool tonight. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Andrew Robertson played nearly 400 games for Liverpool and won countless trophies with the club, including two Premier League titles, two League Cups and the Champions League. Upon his return to Anfield, he starts on the bench against his former employers.

Djaksparo is a rising musician from Paris who who gained viral fame following a social media boost from Liverpool’s summer signing Bradley Barcola, who is on the bench for the hosts this evening.

Welcome to Anfield, Djaksparo 👋 pic.twitter.com/iueYa1KjL7

"I would like to see the goals!"Roberto De Zerbi ahead of Spurs clash with Liverpool in the Carabao Cup 🙌 pic.twitter.com/uSjCJcnAfJ

Richarlison is not happy at Roberto de Zerbi's decision to leave him out of Tottenham's squad tonight 🙅‍♂️ pic.twitter.com/WqRWb3KPed

“There is no joy watching Spurs at the moment. Last year was a survival job, but now you have got to flip it. [Roberto] De Zerbi’s got a lot of players at his disposal.

“He has got to fit that jigsaw puzzle together. There are still a lot of elements that are not right; they have not got a left-sided player they can trust in. Goals have been a real problem, but I do think they will come.”

During the Spaniard’s three seasons at the helm at Bournemouth, he never made it past the fourth round in this competition. He reached the fourth round in his first season at Bournemouth during the 2023/24 season but in the last two seasons has fallen in the second round, which was the round Bournemouth entered the competition.

Just one player remains from Liverpool’s starting XI against Fulham on Saturday and that is Ronald Araujo. Virgil van Dijk and Florian Wirtz are given the night off for the home side.

Roberto De Zerbi makes eight changes from Tottenham’s draw against Everton, with Archie Gray, Rodrigo Bentancur and Omar Marmoush the three players to remain in the starting XI.

We're in the building 🏟️ pic.twitter.com/nPJefN5F3A

Tottenham Hotspur did not pay Roberto De Zerbi, their head coach, a survival bonus for keeping the club in the Premier League and now Spurs are saving a fortune on goal bonuses.

De Zerbi’s team are yet to score against Premier League opposition this season and face Liverpool in the third round of the Carabao Cup at Anfield on Tuesday night.

It is understood that De Zerbi’s lucrative contract did not include a survival bonus for avoiding relegation last season, but he must wish his forwards were cashing in on their goal bonuses.

Peterborough vs Barnsley 7.30pmWest Ham vs Fulham 7.45pmIpswich vs Arsenal 8pmLiverpool vs Tottenham 8pmReading vs Brentford 8pm

Our Spurs side to take on Liverpool 👊🔢 @krakenfx pic.twitter.com/X4f3F0cl4f

Our team to take on Tottenham Hotspur 🔴 pic.twitter.com/tZSJkPpH3y

A place in the League Cup fourth round is at stake at Anfield as Liverpool host Tottenham in an all-Premier League tie.

Liverpool were frustrated on the weekend, being held to a 0-0 draw at home against Fulham, meaning they have one win and three draws from their opening four league games.

“I am very happy with the squad,” Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola said. “I value a lot my players, if we win games, the squad will look amazing and fantastic, if we do not there is going to be a problem with the depth. I think we will see also tomorrow [tonight] players we have not seen still and I am really looking forward to seeing. I feel they are going to play well and help us and they still have not had their chance. You can decide and put the same players in every game. The problem is there will be a moment when they are really tired. And there is more risk of injury.

“But that is why we cannot say it does not work for anyone. There are players who play every three days with no issues. They are very robust, their performances do not change too much. There are other players where the risk is bigger and the performances are different. I have to learn who is ready to play games every three days and who needs a rest so their performance level is not affected. I thought I had it quite clear in my mind with some, but with others, it is new, even for them, because they have not played as many games. We are learning.”

Liverpool were knocked out in the fourth round of this competition last season, losing 3-0 at home against Crystal Palace. Joe Gomez returns to the squad for the hosts tonight after an injury early in pre-season but Giovanni Leoni, Hugo Ekitike, Conor Bradley and Federico Chiesa remain out.

Tottenham are still without a league win or goal this season. Their 0-0 draw at home against Everton Saturday means they sit just above the relegation zone. Tottenham overcame Charlton in the second round, convincingly winning 5-1 at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium last month.

“I think we are working well,” Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi said. “We played 30 minutes, 25 minutes very well [against Everton]. In that moment we could score two goals. Then we lost maybe the confidence because we did not score. For sure we have to improve. For sure I have big confidence in my players, they are very good players.

“We have to improve, yes. We can say the coach has responsibility if we do not score, yes, I accept, no problem. We did not win any game so far, yes. We are disappointed, sorry for that. But we have other positive things, like I said we did not [concede goals] in the last two games and the things we have to improve, we start our work. Nothing changed in my project and my idea.”

Tottenham’s League Cup journey last season came to an end in the fourth round last season, losing 2-0 at Newcastle. Sandro Tonali and Pedro Porro will not be involved tonight for the visitors and neither will Richarlison, who has been left out. Andrew Robertson returns to Anfield for the first time after leaving Liverpool in the summer following nine years on Merseyside.

Team news from Anfield to follow shortly.

#1418. Blues Trio Called Up For England's Nations League Fixtures

Everton trio Jordan Pickford, Jarrad Branthwaite and James Garner have been called up to represent England in the Three Lions’ upcoming Nations League clashes with Croatia and Spain.

Thomas Tuchel’s side sit second in Group C following home and away victories against Czech Republic, with a 7-0 thrashing of Croatia sandwiched in between.

England host Croatia at Wembley on Thursday 12 November (7.45pm GMT) before travelling to face world champions Spain on Sunday 15 November (7.45pm GMT).

Harrison Armstrong and Tyrique George have been called up to represent England's Under-21s as the Young Lions prepare for upcoming games against Portugal and France.

The pair of fixtures will be the group’s first preparation matches ahead of next summer’s UEFA U21 EURO Finals – the young side managed by former-Blue Lee Carsley.

The youngsters secured their place in the Finals last month, and will head to Albania and Serbia in June 2027 with hopes of winning a third successive U21 EURO title.

They will face two nations who will also be heading to the Finals, with Portugal first up at Ashton Gate Stadium on Friday 13 November (7.30pm GMT).

Then, France are the visitors for the second game on Monday 16 November (7.30pm GMT).
